sources.title: Hakenbeck and Buntgen: Drought and Hunnic incursions
sources.note: 2022 study: historical chronology and tree-ring evidence; drought as a proposed contributing factor, not a single cause.

sources.title: Priscus on Attila’s court, translated in the Medieval Sourcebook
sources.note: Priscus translated in 1905: elite homes, banquet and bath. The page’s 448 heading differs from modern dating to 449.

sources.title: Hakenbeck and colleagues: Practising pastoralism in an agricultural environment
sources.note: 2017 primary isotope study of fifth-century Pannonian populations: diet, mobility and changes within individual lifetimes.

sources.title: Mullen and Woudhuysen: Language and history in the late-Roman West
sources.note: 2023 chapter opening: Priscus’s 449 embassy, Greek greeting, multilingual court and interpreters.

sources.title: Marek Stachowski: Slavic languages in contact, 10
sources.note: 2024 article, pp. 56-57: limited Hunnic linguistic evidence, personal names rather than surviving texts or word lists.

sources.title: Zsofia Masek: Hun Period Cauldrons in Hungary
sources.note: 2015 archaeological study: Ocsa fragment, Tortel vessel, uncertain contexts and competing interpretations of vessel use.

sources.title: Pawel Janik: Origins of Hunnic cauldrons
sources.note: Typological study, pp. 43-44: copper or bronze vessels, separately cast sections, soldering and repairs; cultural labels do not identify every maker.

sources.title: Archaeological Museum in Krakow: Jakuszowice grave
sources.note: Early-fifth-century elite burial discovered in 1911; symbolic bow, sword fittings, horse equipment and nearby settlement.

sources.title: Gnecchi-Ruscone and colleagues: European Huns and the Xiongnu Empire
sources.note: 2025 PNAS study, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2418485122: some genetic connections across Eurasia alongside substantial diversity. Ancestry is not an ethnic identity test.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Imported 400-500 coverage is retained and explicitly distinguished from Attila’s death and the breakup around 454.
Priscus embassy dated 449 following modern scholarship rather than the older teaching-page heading.
Regional cemetery evidence does not identify every individual as Hunnic; genetic ancestry is not ethnic identity.
Greek transliterated greeting is clearly identified as Greek; no Hunnic sentence is fabricated.
Household toilets, general medicine and schooling remain unsupported by the selected evidence.

proposedOverrides.name: Hunnic Empire
proposedOverrides.summary: Hunnic power brought varied communities together in fifth-century Europe. Court diplomacy, embroidery and metalwork appear alongside farming and herding. This map interval includes the breakup after Attila’s death; it does not describe a single unchanged empire until 500.
